title: Precision nanomedicine: navigating the tumor microenvironment for enhanced cancer immunotherapy and targeted drug delivery

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Introduction Cancer remains one of the most formidable challenges in modern medicine, with its complexity and heterogeneity posing significant obstacles to effective treatment. Traditional therapies such as chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery have limitations, including systemic toxicity, drug resistance, and incomplete eradication of cancer cells. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative approach, harnessing the body's immune system to target and destroy cancer cells. However, the efficacy of immunotherapy is often hindered by factors within and beyond the TME, such as immunosuppressive conditions, hypoxia, and physical barriers like collagen deposition [ 1 ]. To address these challenges, innovative strategies such as nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery, combination therapies, and personalized medicine are being developed to enhance the precision and effectiveness of cancer therapy. Nanoparticle-based approaches have revolutionized cancer therapy by enabling targeted delivery of therapeutic agents, reducing systemic toxicity, and improving drug bioavailability. These nanocarriers can be engineered to respond to specific stimuli within the TME, such as acidic pH, hypoxia, or overexpressed enzymes, ensuring controlled release of drugs at the tumor site [ 2 ]. For instance, pH-responsive nanoparticles have been designed to release their payload in the acidic TME. At the same time, hypoxia-responsive systems activate under low oxygen conditions to enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy [ 3 ]. Additionally, enzyme-responsive nanoparticles exploit the overexpression of enzymes like matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to achieve site-specific drug release [ 4 ]. Combination therapies, which integrate multiple treatment modalities, have demonstrated great promise in overcoming the limitations of single-agent therapies. By combining immunotherapy with chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, or targeted drug delivery, researchers can simultaneously target multiple pathways involved in tumor growth and resistance. For example, integrating photothermal therapy and immunotherapy using iron oxide nanoplatforms has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in pancreatic cancer treatment [ 5 ]. Similarly, multifunctional nanocarriers that deliver chemotherapeutic agents and immunomodulators can enhance anti-tumor immune responses and improve therapeutic outcomes [ 6 ]. Personalized medicine represents a critical advancement in cancer therapy, leveraging patient-specific biomarkers and genetic profiles to tailor treatments. Machine learning models and quantitative histopathological analyses are being utilized to predict the efficacy of immunotherapies and identify patients who are most likely to benefit from specific treatments [ 7 ]. For instance, mitophagy-related gene signatures in rectal cancer and intestinal subtypes of gastric adenocarcinoma have been identified as predictive biomarkers for immunotherapy response [ 8 ]. These advancements improve treatment efficacy and minimize unnecessary side effects, thus enhancing the overall patients’ quality of life. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in optimizing nanoparticle-mediated therapies and overcoming biological barriers within the TME. The dense extracellular matrix (ECM), interstitial fluid pressure, and immunosuppressive conditions can impede drug delivery and limit therapeutic efficacy [ 9 ]. Therefore, to address these challenges, researchers are developing multifunctional nanoplatforms that combine TME-responsive properties with strategies to enhance drug penetration and modulate the immune response. For example, size-shrinkable nanoparticles that exploit the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect have been designed to penetrate dense tumor tissues. In contrast, iron oxide nanoparticles have been used to repolarize tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from a pro-tumor to an anti-tumor phenotype [ 10 ]. This review focuses on the latest developments in stimuli-responsive nanocarriers (e.g., pH-, redox-, and enzyme-sensitive systems) for tumor-specific drug delivery, emphasizing strategies to overcome biological barriers, including (1) the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect—its role in passive targeting and limitations in heterogeneous tumors, (2) active targeting strategies using ligand-functionalized nanoparticles, and (3) externally triggered systems such as light-, magnetic-, and ultrasound-responsive nanocarriers.

sections.heading: Cancer immunotherapy
sections.text: Cancer immunotherapy Immunotherapy is having a significant impact through innovative strategies, such as nanoparticle-based approaches, combination therapies, and personalized medicine, aimed at addressing the challenges of cancer treatment. Factors both within and beyond the TME have a profound impact on the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Resistance mechanisms in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), for instance, are associated with physical barriers like collagen deposition and hypoxic conditions that hinder T-cell infiltration and suppress the development of lymphoid structures [ 11 ]. Metabolic modulation, including enhancing mannose metabolism, is emerging as a promising approach to improve T-cell stemness and anti-tumor activity [ 12 ]. The PANoptosome pathway appears to be a promising target for immunotherapy, with its activation linked to improved therapeutic responses [ 13 ] (Fig.  1 ). Fig. 1 Various regulated cell death mechanisms—ferroptosis (1), cuproptosis (2), and necroptosis (3)—influence the tumor microenvironment (TME) by shaping immune cell populations and modulating tumor progression. 1) Ferroptosis, characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and requiring GPX4 for protection, triggers the release of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). These signals promote dendritic cell (DC) maturation, enhance antigen presentation, and support cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses while also affecting macrophage polarization (M1 vs. M2). 2) Cuproptosis, a copper-induced cell death mechanism dependent on ASAH2, can activate the cGAS–STING pathway and stimulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ, IL-2). This may boost natural killer (NK) cell and T-cell activity but can also recruit immunosuppressive cells (e.g., regulatory T cells [Tregs], myeloid-derived suppressor cells [MDSCs]) and promote a tolerogenic TME under certain conditions. 3) Necroptosis, driven by the RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL signaling axis, results in cell membrane rupture and additional DAMP release. While this can elicit strong innate and adaptive immune responses—such as NK cell activation and T-cell priming—it may also foster chronic inflammation that supports tumor growth. These distinct death pathways collectively reshape the TME and influence therapeutic outcomes, including responses to immunotherapy. The figure is created with BioRender A primary focus is given to nanoparticle-mediated delivery of immunomodulatory agents, which utilizes stimuli-responsive and combination strategies to boost therapeutic effects. For example, starvation-immunotherapy—combining ultra-long-acting L-asparaginase with checkpoint inhibitors—effectively depletes L-asparagine and inhibits metastasis [ 14 ]. Moreover, extracellular vesicles loaded with IL-12 minicircle plasmids deliver immunostimulatory cytokines directly to tumor cells [ 15 ]. Manganese-coordinated nanoparticles that integrate photosensitizers and STING agonists synergistically activate innate and adaptive immunity via photo-/immuno-therapy [ 16 ]. Precision intelligent nanomissiles transform cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and induce immunogenic cell death, reshaping the TME [ 17 ] (Fig.  2 ). Trinity STING-activating nanoparticles stimulate autologous STING signaling in cancer cells, promoting dendritic cell maturation and T-cell priming [ 18 ]. Peptide-conjugated photodynamic therapy specifically degrades HER2 proteins, enhancing cytotoxic T-cell activity [ 19 ]. Additionally, self-assembled PROTAC nanoparticles are being developed for sustained PD-L1 degradation, which triggers anti-tumor immune responses [ 20 ]. Bioactive nanocomposite hydrogels co-deliver anti-PD-L1 antibodies and other agents, stimulating CD8 + T-cell activity in osteosarcoma [ 21 ]. Furthermore, combined photothermal and hypoxia-activated immunotherapies utilizing nanoparticles can induce immunogenic cell death and reverse immunosuppression [ 22 ]. Fig. 2 The process of normal fibroblasts transforming into CAFs can be described as follows:  a  Growth Factor and cytokine stimulation. Growth factors and cytokines—including transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1), osteopontin (OPN), and IL-1β—bind to their receptors on NFs. This binding trigger downstream effectors such as microRNAs (miRNAs) and CD44, which then regulate CAF-specific gene expression via the TGF-β/Smads and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) pathways.  b  Exosome-Mediated Transformation: Exosomes released by cancer cells, carrying cargos like miRNAs and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), convert NFs into CAFs. They do so by activating several signaling cascades, including TGF-β/Smads, Janus kinase/signal transducers and activators of transcription (JAK/STAT), NF-κB, and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways.  c  Metabolic Reprogramming: The conversion is also driven by a reprogramming of glucose metabolism. The hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) signaling pathway promotes glycolysis during this transformation.  d  Homeostasis disruption: Shifts in cellular homeostasis trigger a self-sustaining conversion by modulating the activation of cytoskeletal proteins and altering the cell’s secretory phenotype through the JAK/STAT and p53 pathways. Additional regulatory elements in this conversion process include factors such as Fli-1 leukemia integration 1, transcription factor 12 (TCF12), suppressor of cytokine signaling (1SOCS1), β−1,4-galactosyltransferases III (B4GALT3), insulin-like growth factor 2 receptor (IGF2R), lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC), Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1), TEA domain transcription factor-1 (TEAD1), stromal cell-derived factor-1 (SDF-1), epiregulin (EREG), and reactive oxygen species (ROS). The figure is created with BioRender Personalized immunotherapy is advancing through the identification of prognostic and predictive biomarkers. For instance, the mitophagy-related gene signatures in rectal cancer present promising avenues for tailored therapeutic approaches [ 23 ]. Moreover, the intestinal subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma, coupled with machine learning models, has demonstrated reliability in predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy [ 24 ]. Machine learning classifiers that forecast tumor-reactive T-cell receptors are accelerating the development of personalized T-cell therapies [ 25 ]. Furthermore, quantitative histopathological analyses and radiomic models derived from computed tomography (CT) scans provide non-invasive techniques to predict the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy and the expression of PD-L1, thereby enhancing patient stratification [ 26 ]. Nevertheless, patient-specific factors, such as cancer cachexia and associated weight loss, significantly influence the outcomes of CAR T-cell therapy [ 27 ]. However, not all combination immunotherapies yield beneficial results, as evidenced by the lack of efficacy of adjuvant nivolumab/ipilimumab in gastro-oesophageal adenocarcinoma [ 28 ]. Interestingly, innovative strategies are being devised to refine cancer treatments, emphasizing targeted genome editing, organoid models, and nanoparticle-based therapies to enhance immune responses and counteract immunosuppression. A multiple cancer-targeting genome editing system that utilizes aptamer-decorated nanoparticles effectively knocks out MUC1 and downregulates PD-L1 in circulating malignant cells, which leads to an increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, thereby demonstrating a personalized approach to treatment [ 29 ]. Patient-derived glioblastoma organoids (GBOs) act as real-time patient avatars, reflecting responses to CAR-T cell therapy and providing critical insights into CAR-T cell bioactivity and treatment efficacy [ 30 ]. To reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, engineered gold nanoparticles have been designed to regulate oncogenic microRNAs on demand and execute RNA-dependent photothermal immunotherapy, effectively inhibiting PD-1/PD-L1-mediated immune evasion while generating tumor-associated antigens to activate anti-tumor T cells [ 31 ]. Additionally, natural compounds appear promising; for example, Ginkgolide B demonstrates efficacy by targeting the SREBP1/KLK8/CCL22 axis, effectively preventing immune escape in oral squamous cell carcinoma [ 32 ]. Multiplex immunohistochemical analysis of samples from head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) has uncovered that the presence of T cells, particularly CD4 + and CD8 + T cell subsets, can predict responses to neoadjuvant immunotherapy, with TIM3 + and LAG3 + T cells demonstrating diminished levels in responders post-treatment [ 33 ]. The expression of extracellular HSP90α in driver-gene-negative non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) correlates with prognosis and the efficacy of immunotherapy, marking it as a potential predictive biomarker [ 34 ]. Tumor-selective nano-dispatchers that regulate lactate metabolism while activating Toll-like receptors have been reported to enhance the effects of cancer immunotherapy by decreasing lactate levels within the TME and promoting T-cell infiltration [ 35 ]. Moreover, in metastatic synovial sarcomas, the prevalence and co-expression of cancer-testis antigens, such as MAGE-A4 and NY-ESO-1, provide crucial insights for developing targeted T-cell therapies [ 36 ]. Moreover, HPK1 kinase inhibitors have been identified as sufficient for selectively targeting HPK1 in T-cell-mediated cancer immunotherapy, presenting a more straightforward alternative compared with HPK1 degraders [ 37 ]. In addition, pan-cancer and experimental studies emphasize the significance of CST2, linked with stomach adenocarcinoma proliferation and metastasis, thereby suggesting its potential as a therapeutic target [ 38 ].
